notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether hand can be divided into groups of groupSize consecutive integers.
Idea: Count card frequencies and repeatedly form a group starting at the smallest remaining value.
Technique and why it applies: Every group must start at the smallest remaining value; otherwise that value could never be used. The code decrements each consecutive frequency and removes a value from the min-heap when its count reaches zero.
Invariant: freq stores remaining card counts and min_heap tracks candidate smallest values.
Edge cases: The snippet uses collections.defaultdict and heapq without imports, so those names must be supplied externally. The length must be divisible by groupSize.
Complexity: Heap operations and group scans give roughly O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether hand can be rearranged into groups of W consecutive numbers.
Idea: Count values, heapify all cards, and use each smallest remaining card to start a group.
Technique and why it applies: A group beginning at start consumes start,start+1,...,start+W-1. Negative remaining counts immediately reveal an impossible grouping; stale heap entries are skipped.
Invariant: counts tracks unused copies of each value, and the heap provides the next smallest possible group start.
Edge cases: If len(hand) is not divisible by W, return False. The heap includes duplicate values, which are skipped after their frequency reaches zero.
Complexity: Heapify is O(n), and each card is popped at most once; group processing is O(nW) in a loose bound, with O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest path that visits every node in an undirected graph.
Idea: Compute all-pairs shortest distances, then memoize a subset-DP recurrence over the current node and remaining-node bitmask.
Technique and why it applies: Floyd–Warshall computes distances between every pair. The recursion chooses the next node to visit and adds the shortest-path distance plus the remaining DP cost.
Invariant: fn(x,mask) is intended to be the minimum cost from x to visit the nodes represented by mask.
Edge cases: The code uses inf and cache without imports in the snippet, so those names must be supplied externally. The initial mask includes x, allowing a zero-cost self visit before other nodes.
Complexity: Floyd–Warshall costs O(n³); subset DP has O(n·2^n) states and O(n) transitions per state, for O(n²2^n) time and O(n2^n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the shortest walk visiting every node in an undirected graph.
Idea: Run BFS over states consisting of a visited-node bitmask and current node, starting from every node.
Technique and why it applies: Each move follows one graph edge and adds its destination to the bitmask. BFS explores these states by path length, and the full-mask states represent walks that have visited all nodes.
Invariant: dp[mask][node] stores the shortest number of steps reaching node with exactly the visited mask.
Edge cases: Multi-source initialization handles any optimal starting node. The graph is assumed connected as specified by the problem.
Complexity: There are O(n·2^n) states and each explores incident edges, giving O(2^n(n+E)) time and O(n2^n) space.

Task and constraints: Apply cumulative leftward shifts to each letter of s.
Idea: Compute suffix sums of shifts modulo 26 and apply each accumulated shift to its corresponding character.
Technique and why it applies: A shift at index i affects every character at or before i. Summing shifts from right to left produces the total offset for each character, and subtracting 26 wraps values back into lowercase letters.
Invariant: nums[i] is the cumulative shift affecting s[i].
Edge cases: Each character is lowercase English, so at most one subtraction of 26 is needed after adding a shift modulo 26.
Complexity: Two linear passes give O(n) time and O(n) space for suffix sums and output.

Task and constraints: Shift each character by the sum of shifts from its position through the end.
Idea: Maintain a rolling suffix-shift total while scanning left to right.
Technique and why it applies: times begins as the sum of all shifts modulo 26. After emitting the current shifted character, subtracting shifts[i] leaves the total affecting the next character.
Invariant: times is the sum of shifts for the current index and all later indices, modulo 26.
Edge cases: Modulo handles shifts larger than 26 and wraps z back to a. The input is assumed lowercase.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Find the seat with maximum distance to the nearest occupied seat.
Idea: Collect occupied positions and compare the empty leading/trailing segments with half the gaps between occupied seats.
Technique and why it applies: At an interior gap of length y-x-1, the best seat is near its midpoint, giving distance floor((y-x)/2). At the ends, the distance is the number of empty seats before the first or after the last occupied seat.
Invariant: seat_nums is the sorted list of occupied indices.
Edge cases: The code assumes at least one occupied seat because min and max are called on seat_nums. It uses integer floor division for gap distances.
Complexity: Collecting seats and scanning gaps take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum possible distance from an empty seat to the closest occupied seat.
Idea: Scan occupied seats and track the distance to the previous occupied seat.
Technique and why it applies: The first occupied seat determines the left-edge distance; each later gap contributes half its length, and the final suffix determines the right-edge distance.
Invariant: prev is the most recent occupied index and result is the best distance among processed gaps.
Edge cases: The input is assumed to contain at least one occupied seat. If seats are all zero, the initial prev logic would return len(seats), which is outside the intended constraints.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the union area of axis-aligned rectangles modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Sweep horizontal y-levels and maintain the total covered x-length using a segment tree.
Technique and why it applies: Each rectangle creates an opening event at y1 and a closing event at y2. Between events, covered x-length is constant, so area increases by delta-y times that length. Segment-tree counts mark covered intervals.
Invariant: st.total[1] is the covered x-length at the current sweep level.
Edge cases: The code uses defaultdict without importing it. Its update call uses tr=len(xs)-1 while total accesses xs[tr+1], which can index beyond the compressed coordinate array when a fully covered node is updated.
Complexity: Sorting 2n events is O(n log n); segment updates are O(log n) each, with O(n) tree storage.

Task and constraints: Find the union area of all rectangles, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Sweep rectangle opening and closing events by y-coordinate while updating a segment tree over compressed x intervals.
Technique and why it applies: Between successive y values, the covered x-length is fixed. Multiplying it by the vertical gap adds that strip's union area; the segment tree tracks coverage counts and covered length.
Invariant: cur_x_sum is the covered horizontal length after processing the current event.
Edge cases: Rectangles are assumed nonempty. The tree uses half-open compressed intervals, so x endpoints are represented as indices and the right endpoint is excluded.
Complexity: Event sorting and O(log n) updates give O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: For each person, find the quietest person who is at least as rich, including themselves.
Idea: Topologically process the richer-than graph and propagate the quietest known person to poorer neighbors.
Technique and why it applies: Edges point from richer to poorer. Once a richer node is processed, its quietest candidate can be compared with the current candidate for each poorer node.
Invariant: arr[v] is the index of the quietest person known among v and richer people already propagated to it.
Edge cases: The code uses collections.defaultdict and collections.deque without importing collections, so it requires an external import. The graph is assumed acyclic because richer relationships form a partial order.
Complexity: Topological traversal is O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space.

Task and constraints: Find the peak index in a strictly increasing-then-decreasing mountain array.
Idea: Binary-search using the comparison between arr[mid] and arr[mid+1].
Technique and why it applies: On the increasing slope, the peak is to the right; on the decreasing slope, it is at mid or left. The search bounds shrink until beg identifies the peak.
Invariant: The peak remains inside the candidate interval.
Edge cases: The code assumes a valid mountain array with at least three elements, so there is no flat slope. The strict shape prevents the loop from evaluating an invalid final successor.
Complexity: Binary search takes O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the peak index of a mountain array.
Idea: Compare the midpoint with its successor and move toward the rising or falling side.
Technique and why it applies: If arr[mid] exceeds arr[mid+1], the peak is at or left of mid; otherwise it is to the right. The interval is narrowed until the peak index is located.
Invariant: [left,right] always contains the unique peak.
Edge cases: The input is guaranteed to be a mountain array, preventing an invalid flat-top case. The loop's midpoint comparisons remain within bounds under that guarantee.
Complexity: The search is O(log n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Count car fleets that arrive at target.
Idea: Sort cars from nearest to target to farthest and compare their arrival times.
Technique and why it applies: A car with a greater arrival time than the fleet ahead cannot catch it and starts a new fleet. A car arriving sooner or at the same time joins the fleet ahead.
Invariant: arrival_bound is the arrival time of the closest fleet already encountered.
Edge cases: Cars are assumed to have distinct starting positions and positive speeds. Floating-point arrival times avoid integer truncation.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), scanning O(n), and auxiliary space O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps needed to transform s1 into s2, which are anagrams.
Idea: Use memoized recursion, fixing the first mismatched index by swapping in a character that matches s2 there.
Technique and why it applies: Swapping a later needed character into the first mismatch makes that position correct. The recursive state advances to the next index and caches results by index and current string.
Invariant: helper(i,curr) returns the minimum swaps needed to fix the suffix beginning at i.
Edge cases: The code uses sys.maxsize without importing sys in the snippet. If s1 already equals s2, the base case returns zero.
Complexity: The number of distinct intermediate strings can be factorial in length, so worst-case time and memo space are exponential/factorial.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum swaps to make an anagram A equal B.
Idea: BFS over string states, swapping a character into the first position where the current string differs from B.
Technique and why it applies: At the first mismatch i, only later characters equal to B[i] are useful swap candidates. BFS guarantees the first target state found uses the fewest swaps.
Invariant: Each queue layer contains strings reachable with the same number of swaps.
Edge cases: The code does not add the initial A to lookup, so it may enqueue A again once, but the target is checked before expanding each state. A==B returns zero.
Complexity: The number of distinct states can be factorial in string length, with exponential/factorial time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the score of a balanced parentheses string using the rules for () and nested pairs.
Idea: Track nesting depth and add a power of two whenever a primitive pair () closes.
Technique and why it applies: A pair closing immediately after an opening parenthesis contributes 2^(depth-1). Each primitive pair at depth d receives the multiplicative score induced by its nesting.
Invariant: level is the current nesting depth, and result accumulates contributions from all immediate () pairs.
Edge cases: The code assumes a valid balanced parentheses string. prev detects whether the current closing parenthesis completes an immediate pair.
Complexity: One scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Evaluate the score of a balanced parentheses string.
Idea: Use a stack of partial scores, pushing a new frame for each opening parenthesis.
Technique and why it applies: On a closing parenthesis, an empty inner frame scores one; a nonempty inner frame scores twice its accumulated score. The value is added to the enclosing frame.
Invariant: Each stack entry is the score accumulated inside its corresponding open parenthesis level.
Edge cases: The string is assumed balanced, so every closing parenthesis has a matching stack frame. The initial zero frame accumulates top-level concatenated scores.
Complexity: Each character is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

Task and constraints: Return the score of a balanced parentheses string.
Idea: Track nesting depth and add a power of two whenever a closing parenthesis immediately follows an opening parenthesis.
Technique and why it applies: A primitive () at depth d contributes 2^d after depth is decreased, which accounts for the doubling at each enclosing level. Other closing parentheses only reduce depth.
Invariant: depth is the nesting level after processing the current character, and result sums all primitive-pair contributions.
Edge cases: The method assumes valid parentheses. The expression S[i-1] is safe for a valid string because the first character cannot be a closing parenthesis.
Complexity: One pass is O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Minimize the total cost of hiring k workers under a common wage-to-quality ratio.
Idea: Sort workers by wage/quality ratio and maintain a max-heap of the k smallest qualities.
Technique and why it applies: At a given ratio, the total pay is ratio times the selected quality sum. If a new worker has smaller quality than the heap maximum, replacing the largest quality reduces total cost.
Invariant: pq contains the selected qualities as negatives, and kSmallest is their sum.
Edge cases: The snippet uses heapq.heappush, heappop, and heappush without importing them; it needs those names externally. It assumes k is valid and qualities are positive.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), heap updates O(n log k), and space is O(n).
